hook.support: You tell your mates about a good job. Then you tell your nan. Do you use the same words? No. Good speakers change their words to suit who is listening.
hook.core: Explain why you want to get your Ls: once to your mates, once to your parents, once to a driving instructor. Same goal, three different talks. Good speakers don’t just know their topic. They know who’s listening, and they choose every word for that crowd.
hook.extend: Strong speakers start with the audience. What do they already know? What do they care about? What will move them? Your words, and your mix of logic, reasoning and emotion, should follow from that.

why.support: The right words help people listen to you.
why.core: Whether you’re giving advice at work, speaking at a club or talking to a boss, choosing words for your audience decides whether they listen.
why.extend: Thinking about your audience is the first step in any talk that gives advice or tries to persuade. You’ll need it at work, in your community and in public debate.

articles.title: Who’s listening?

body.support:
Your **audience** is the people listening to you. Good speakers think about them first.

**Ask three questions:**
- What do they already know?
- What do they care about?
- What do I want them to do?
.
**Choose your words.**
- With mates, you can be **informal**. “It’s heaps good.”.
- With a boss, be more **formal**. “It works well.”.
- With kids, use short, simple words.
.
**Use a mix of three things:**
- **Logic:** facts and numbers.
- **Reasoning:** explain why. “Because… so…”.
- **Emotion:** a story or feeling.
.
Some people want facts. Some people want a story. Most people need both.
body.core:
Your **audience** is the people you’re speaking to. Before you plan a single word, think about them.

**Three questions:**
- **What do they know?** Experts get bored by basics. Beginners get lost in **jargon**.
- **What do they care about?** Parents care about safety. Bosses care about cost and time. Teens care about freedom and their mates.
- **What do I want them to do?** Agree? Act? Change a habit?
.
**Language choice.** The words you choose change how people react.
- **Formal** or **informal**: “Good morning, everyone” or “Hey, legends”?
- Simple or technical words.
- “You” speaks to them. “We” brings them in.
- Strong words stir feelings: “dangerous” hits harder than “not ideal”.
.
**Logic, reasoning and emotion.** Speakers persuade with a mix of:
- **Logic:** facts, numbers and evidence.
- **Reasoning:** linking ideas so they make sense. “Because… so… which means…”.
- **Emotion:** stories, images and feelings like pride, fear or hope.
.
The right mix depends on the audience. A safety officer might lead with logic. A coach before a grand final might lead with emotion. The best talks use all three.
body.extend:
An **audience** shapes every choice in a talk. Before planning content, effective speakers analyse:
- **knowledge:** what the audience already knows, and what **jargon** they share.
- **values and concerns:** what matters to them, such as safety, money, fairness, belonging or status.
- **attitude:** whether they are likely to agree, disagree or not care.
- **purpose:** what you want them to think, feel or do afterwards.

**Language choice** follows from that analysis:
- **register:** formal or informal, technical or plain.
- **pronouns:** “you” for direct address; **inclusive language** (“we”, “us”, “our”) to build unity.
- **connotation:** words carry feelings as well as meanings (“reckless” or “risky”, “invest” or “spend”).
- **examples:** chosen from the audience’s own world.

**Logic, reasoning and emotion.** Persuasive speakers combine three tools:
- **logic:** facts, statistics and evidence.
- **reasoning:** cause and effect, comparisons and step-by-step explanation.
- **emotion:** stories, vivid images and appeals to feelings and values.

Too much logic can feel cold. Too much emotion can feel manipulative. The balance should suit the audience and the occasion. A hostile audience often needs evidence first. A sympathetic one may respond more to a story.

After speaking, **evaluate your own choices**: what landed, what didn’t, and why?

caseStudies.title: One speech, many audiences

body.support:
On **13 February 2008**, the Prime Minister, **Kevin Rudd**, gave a speech. He said **sorry** to the **Stolen Generations**.

These are First Nations people who were taken from their families as kids.

Many people heard the speech:
- people who were taken as kids.
- the people in Parliament.
- millions of people watching on TV.

He told the true story of one woman. Her name was **Nanna Nungala Fejo**. She was taken from her family when she was a little girl. Her story helped people feel what happened.

He also gave reasons. He said why the nation needed to say sorry.
body.core:
On **13 February 2008**, the Prime Minister, **Kevin Rudd**, made a formal **apology** in Parliament. It was to the **Stolen Generations**. These are First Nations children who were taken from their families by governments.

The speech had many audiences at once. Some people from the Stolen Generations sat in Parliament House. Politicians from all parties were there. Thousands of people stood outside. Millions watched live on TV.

Rudd used **emotion**. He told the true story of **Nanna Nungala Fejo**. She was taken from her family as a young girl. One story helped people imagine what happened to many.

He used **reasoning** too. He said why the apology was needed, and why it mattered for the future.

His words were formal. He spoke for “we”, the nation. He spoke to “you”, the Stolen Generations.
body.extend:
On **13 February 2008**, the Prime Minister, **Kevin Rudd**, gave the **National Apology** to the **Stolen Generations**. These are First Nations children who were taken from their families under past government laws.

Few speeches have had so many audiences at once. In Parliament House sat members of the Stolen Generations and their families. Politicians from all parties were in the room. Outside, thousands gathered. Millions watched live across the country.

The speech mixed **emotion** and **reasoning**. Rudd told the story of **Nanna Nungala Fejo**, who was taken from her family as a young child. One personal story made a national history feel real. He then gave reasons why an apology was needed, and what it should lead to.

His **language choices** suited a formal, national event. He used “we” to speak for the nation. He used “you” to speak straight to the Stolen Generations.

The National Museum of Australia lists the Apology as one of the nation’s defining moments.

model.text:
**Topic:** why young people should learn first aid.
**Audience 1: Year 10 students**
“Who here has seen someone get hurt at footy, or at a party? Most of us just freeze. A first aid course takes one day. It means next time, you’re the one who knows what to do.”
**Audience 2: the school council**
“Good evening. Young people are often first on the scene, at sport, at work and at home. A one-day first aid course would give every Year 10 student the skills to help. We’re asking the council to fund it.”
**What I changed:** for students, I used a question and a feeling. For the council, I used formal words, reasons and a clear ask.
why: The student version opens with a question from their world.
The council version uses formal words and a clear request.
The final note explains each change and why.

teacher.overview: Students learn to analyse an audience (knowledge, values, purpose), choose language for it (formality, jargon, pronouns, strong words) and combine logic, reasoning and emotion. They write the opening of a talk twice for two audiences and explain their changes. The case study is the 2008 National Apology to the Stolen Generations, which addressed several audiences at once using a personal story, reasoning and inclusive language.
prep: Read the case study and plan for it carefully: some students may have family connections to the Stolen Generations. Consult your Koorie Engagement Support Officer or First Nations staff if possible.
Optional: show a short, appropriate clip of the Apology (the National Museum of Australia has resources).

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 question from the audience’s world; 2 story (emotion); 3 checkable fact (logic); 4 cause and effect (reasoning); 5 inclusive “we”; 6 a clear ask in their language.

**Sort:** logic — helmet law; cost comparison. Reasoning — head hits first so helmet takes the hit; “if you can’t afford a new head”. Emotion — little brother in hospital; mate who can’t remember.

**Case study:** audiences were members of the Stolen Generations, politicians, crowds outside and millions watching; Nanna Fejo’s story made the history personal; reasoning explained why an apology was needed; “we” spoke for the nation, “you” addressed the Stolen Generations.

**Note:** the P1 peer-passenger rule in the diagram reflects VicRoads rules at time of writing; check current rules.

resources.label: National Museum of Australia — National Apology

realityCheck: **The case study is about real trauma.** Some students or families may be directly affected. Frame it respectfully, don’t ask students to share family history, and know your support pathways.
**Keep the focus on how the speech works,** not on debating whether the Apology was right.
**Check the P-plate passenger rule** in the diagram against current VicRoads rules before teaching.
**Works in a real class:** yes. “Mates vs nan” is an instantly understood hook.
